about: Three courses fused, grouped by idea: Halbleiterphysik after Strasser (2015), Skriptum Halbleiterphysik, TU Wien; Elektronische Bauelemente after its exercise collection, Hobler (2009); and Schaltungstechnik after Zimmermann (2010), Skriptum Schaltungstechnik, with the worked examples of Schneider & Zimmermann (2005). Pages of the Schaltungstechnik script (ST) are its printed pages, PDF page minus 6. Bode and Nyquist theory is left to the Automation lab. Every equation was read in the scripts on 1 Nov 2026; its section and printed page are given, with the equation number where the script prints one next to it. Practice questions come from the two courses' exercise sheets; those marked 'worked by hand' were solved here from the script's equations, the others agree with the course's worked solutions, whose page is named. tests/unit/labs-data.test.js recomputes each answer with the core and fails if they disagree.

lectures.heading: Worked example
lectures.title: A 25 W amplifier, from the supply to the heat sink

labs.title: Energy bands from coupled wells
labs.idea: One well has sharp levels; N wells side by side split each level into N; a crystal's many wells fill whole bands, separated by gaps.

equations.note: two coupled states, bonding and anti-bonding
wave numbers in the well and in the barrier

equations.eq: (β² − α²)/(2αβ) sinh(βb) sin(αa) + cosh(βb) cos(αa) = cos(k(a + b))
P sin(αa)/(αa) + cos(αa) = cos(ka), P = m a V0 b/ħ²
equations.tex: P\,\frac{\sin(\alpha a)}{\alpha a} + \cos(\alpha a) = \cos(ka), \qquad P = \frac{ma}{\hbar^2}V_0 b
equations.note: thin, high barriers; bands where the left side lies in [−1, 1]
P → ∞: the levels of the infinite well

equations.eq: ψ′ jumps by (2P/a) ψ at each barrier
equations.note: the thin-barrier limit of (2.2.12), from the Schrödinger equation integrated across V0 b δ(x); the transfer matrix used for N wells and as the second route

practice.question: A GaAs layer 10 nm thick between AlAs is a quantum well for electrons, m* = 0.067 m0. In the infinite-well approximation, what is the lowest subband's energy above the band edge?
practice.solution: E1 = π²ħ²/(2 m* a²) = 9.87 × (1.055·10⁻³⁴ J s)² / (2 × 0.067 × 9.11·10⁻³¹ kg × 10⁻¹⁶ m²) = 8.99·10⁻²¹ J = 56 meV. It is the P → ∞ limit of this lab, where each band shrinks onto n² E1.
practice.source: Worked by hand from Halbleiterphysik exercise sheet 10, problem 38 a (WS 2015/16), with Strasser (2015), section 2.2.3

labs.title: Fermi–Dirac occupation
labs.idea: Each state holds one electron at most: at 0 K every state below the Fermi level is full and every one above empty; warmth softens the edge over a few kT.

equations.note: Maxwell–Boltzmann, two levels with equal numbers of states
the non-degenerate approximation, for E − EF of several kT

practice.question: What is the probability that a state 0.1 eV above the Fermi level is occupied at 300 K?
practice.solution: kT = 25.85 meV at 300 K, so (E − EF)/kT = 3.87 and f = 1/(1 + e^3.87) = 1/48.9 = 0.0205. The Boltzmann approximation gives e^−3.87 = 0.0209, already within 2 %.
practice.source: Worked by hand from Strasser (2015), section 3.1.2

labs.title: Carrier density and the Fermi level
labs.idea: Doping sets the majority density; mass action fixes the minority one; heat raises ni until the sample turns intrinsic and the Fermi level returns to mid-gap.
labs.law: n p = ni² = NC NV e^(−Eg/kT)
labs.lecture: Strasser (2015), sections 3.1.2–3.1.3, pp. 82–85; material data p. 73

equations.eq: n = NC exp(−(EC − EF)/kT), NC = 2(2π mn* kT)^(3/2)/h³
ni² = n p = NC NV exp(−(EC − EV)/kT)
equations.note: mass action; ni = 1.45·10¹⁰ cm⁻³ for Si at 300 K (table p. 73)

equations.eq: n = ni exp((EF − Ei)/kT), p = ni exp((Ei − EF)/kT)
equations.tex: n = n_\mathrm{i}\exp\!\Big(\frac{E_\mathrm{F} - E_\mathrm{i}}{kT}\Big), \qquad p = n_\mathrm{i}\exp\!\Big(\frac{E_\mathrm{i} - E_\mathrm{F}}{kT}\Big)

equations.note: from (3.1.17) and (3.1.20) with Eg held constant

practice.question: Silicon at 300 K is doped with ND = 10¹⁶ cm⁻³ donors. What is the hole density p?
practice.solution: n ≈ ND = 10¹⁶ cm⁻³ since ND ≫ ni; p = ni²/n = (1.45·10¹⁰)²/10¹⁶ = 2.1·10⁴ cm⁻³ (3.1.24).
practice.source: Worked by hand from Strasser (2015), section 3.1.3, with ni from the table on p. 73

practice.question: How far above the intrinsic level Ei does the Fermi level lie in that sample?
practice.source: Worked by hand from Strasser (2015), section 3.1.2

labs.title: Drift and diffusion
labs.idea: A pulse of minority carriers moves with the field (drift), spreads by itself (diffusion) and fades (recombination): the Shockley–Haynes experiment shows all three at once.
labs.law: Jp = e p µp E − e Dp dp/dx

equations.note: conductivity from both carriers; the script writes q here and e elsewhere

equations.eq: Jp = e p µp E − e Dp dp/dx, Jn = e n µn E + e Dn dn/dx

equations.tex: \frac{\partial p}{\partial t} - D_\mathrm{p}\frac{\partial^2 p}{\partial x^2} + \mu_\mathrm{p}E\frac{\partial p}{\partial x} + \frac{p - p_0}{\tau_\mathrm{L}} = 0

equations.eq: p − p0 = const/√(4πDp t) · exp(−(x − µp E t)²/(4 Dp t)) · exp(−t/τL)
equations.note: its solution, a drifting Gaussian; the script prints both exponents without their minus signs, a misprint (its text says the area decays as exp(−t/τL))

practice.question: A silicon photoconductor is doped n-type, ND = 5·10¹⁵ cm⁻³, 100 µm long, 100 µm wide and 1 µm thick. What is its resistance in the dark at 300 K?
practice.solution: σ = e ND µn = 1.602·10⁻¹⁹ × 5·10¹⁵ × 1500 = 1.20 S/cm; R = L/(σ w d) = 0.01 cm / (1.20 S/cm × 0.01 cm × 10⁻⁴ cm) = 8.32 kΩ. Mobility from the script's table, p. 73.
practice.source: Worked by hand from Halbleiterphysik exercise sheet 10, problem 37 a (WS 2015/16)

practice.question: Holes in n-silicon (µp = 450 cm²/(V s)) are injected and collected 5 mm further on, with a field of 10 V/cm. When does the pulse's peak arrive?
practice.solution: The peak moves at µp E = 450 × 10 = 4500 cm/s (3.4.43); 0.5 cm / 4500 cm/s = 111 µs.
practice.source: Worked by hand from Strasser (2015), section 3.4.5

labs.title: Generation, recombination and lifetime
labs.idea: Light makes electron–hole pairs; they recombine with the minority-carrier lifetime τ. In time the excess settles at Gτ; in space it reaches a diffusion length L = √(Dτ).

equations.tex: \frac{\partial p}{\partial t} + \frac{1}{e}\frac{\partial J_\mathrm{p}}{\partial x} = G - R

equations.eq: Δp(t) = Gτ(1 − e^(−t/τ)), then Δp(toff) e^(−(t − toff)/τ)
equations.note: uniform light switched on and off

equations.eq: pn(x) = pn0 + (pn(0) − pn0) e^(−x/Lp), Lp = √(Dp τL)

equations.note: a sample much shorter than Lp

practice.question: The photoconductor of the drift lab (ND = 5·10¹⁵ cm⁻³, 100 µm × 100 µm × 1 µm) is lit uniformly with G = 8·10²¹ cm⁻³ s⁻¹; the lifetime is 10 µs. What is its resistance now?
practice.solution: Δn = Δp = Gτ = 8·10¹⁶ cm⁻³. σ = e[(ND + Δn) µn + Δp µp] = 1.602·10⁻¹⁹ × (8.5·10¹⁶ × 1500 + 8·10¹⁶ × 450) = 26.2 S/cm; R = L/(σ w d) = 382 Ω. Mobilities from the script's table, p. 73.
practice.source: Worked by hand from Halbleiterphysik exercise sheet 10, problem 37 b (WS 2015/16)

practice.question: Holes in silicon at 300 K (µp = 450 cm²/(V s)) live 10 µs. What is their diffusion length?
practice.source: Worked by hand from Strasser (2015), section 3.4.4

labs.title: Optical absorption at the band gap
labs.idea: A photon is absorbed only if it can lift an electron across the gap; in a direct semiconductor the absorption grows as the square root of the excess energy, and with enough injected carriers it turns into gain.
labs.law: α(ω) = σ Zj(ω) (fv(E1) − fc(E2)),  Zj ∝ √(ħω − Eg)
labs.lecture: Strasser (2015), section 4.2.1, pp. 113–117; material data p. 73

equations.eq: E2 − E1 = ħ²k²/(2mp*) + Eg + ħ²k²/(2mn*) = ħω
E1 = EV − (mr/mp*)(ħω − Eg), E2 = EC + (mr/mn*)(ħω − Eg), 1/mr = 1/mp* + 1/mn*
equations.tex: E_1 = E_\mathrm{V} - \frac{m_\mathrm{r}}{m_\mathrm{p}^*}(\hbar\omega - E_\mathrm{G}), \qquad E_2 = E_\mathrm{C} + \frac{m_\mathrm{r}}{m_\mathrm{n}^*}(\hbar\omega - E_\mathrm{G}), \qquad \frac{1}{m_\mathrm{r}} = \frac{1}{m_\mathrm{p}^*} + \frac{1}{m_\mathrm{n}^*}
equations.note: the states taking part; the script prints E2 = EC − …, a misprint: only + gives E2 − E1 = ħω of (4.2.2)

practice.question: Silicon's band gap is 1.12 eV. What is the longest wavelength it absorbs across the gap?
practice.solution: λ = hc/Eg = 6.626·10⁻³⁴ J s × 2.998·10⁸ m/s / (1.12 × 1.602·10⁻¹⁹ J) = 1107 nm, as the script's table prints beside 1.12 eV (p. 73).
practice.source: Worked by hand; the script's table on p. 73 prints the same 1107 nm

practice.question: In GaAs (Eg = 1.42 eV, mn* = 0.067 m0, mp* = 0.5 m0) a photon of 1.52 eV is absorbed. How far above the conduction band edge does the electron land?
practice.solution: 1/mr = 1/0.067 + 1/0.5 = 16.93, mr = 0.0591 m0; E2 − EC = (mr/mn*)(ħω − Eg) = 0.882 × 0.1 eV = 88 meV. The hole takes the other 12 meV.
practice.source: Worked by hand from Halbleiterphysik exercise sheet 10, problem 39 (WS 2015/16), its GaAs data, with Strasser (2015), p. 114

labs.title: The pn junction's space-charge zone
labs.idea: Where p meets n, the carriers leave and the ionised dopants stay: a charge double layer, a triangular field and a potential step UD − U. The zone grows into the lighter-doped side.
labs.lecture: Strasser (2015), section 5.2.1, pp. 128–131; UD from section 5.3.4, p. 139

equations.eq: Emax = e NA dp/ε = e ND dn/ε
equations.note: the peak field at the boundary, as a magnitude (the script drops its minus sign from p. 131 on)

equations.eq: d = √(2ε(UD − U)/(e N0)), dn = d NA/(NA + ND), dp = d ND/(NA + ND), Emax = √(2eN0(UD − U)/ε)
equations.tex: d = \sqrt{\frac{2\varepsilon(U_\mathrm{D} - U)}{eN_0}}, \quad d_\mathrm{n} = d\,\frac{N_\mathrm{A}}{N_\mathrm{A} + N_\mathrm{D}}, \quad d_\mathrm{p} = d\,\frac{N_\mathrm{D}}{N_\mathrm{A} + N_\mathrm{D}}, \quad E_\mathrm{max} = \sqrt{\frac{2eN_0(U_\mathrm{D} - U)}{\varepsilon}}

practice.question: A silicon junction has NA = 10¹⁷ cm⁻³ and ND = 10¹⁵ cm⁻³ at 300 K, no bias. How wide is its space-charge zone? (εr = 11.9)
practice.source: Worked by hand from Strasser (2015), section 5.2.1

labs.title: Junction capacitance
labs.idea: The space-charge zone is a plate capacitor whose gap widens with reverse bias, so the capacitance falls as 1/√(UD − U): a voltage-tuned capacitor, and a way to measure doping.
labs.law: Cs = εA/d = A √(ε e N0 / (2(UD − U)))
labs.lecture: Strasser (2015), section 5.2.2, pp. 131–132; breakdown section 5.3.5, p. 140

equations.eq: Cs = dQp/dU = εA/d = A √(ε e N0/(2(UD − U)))

equations.note: a straight line in U; its slope gives N0
the breakdown estimate; Emax ≈ 300 kV/cm for Si

practice.question: A silicon p⁺n diode has NA = 10¹⁹ cm⁻³, ND = 10¹⁶ cm⁻³ and an area of 0.01 mm². What is its junction capacitance at 5 V reverse bias?
practice.source: Worked by hand from Strasser (2015), section 5.2.2

labs.title: The diode characteristic
labs.idea: Forward bias injects minority carriers that diffuse away: the current grows exponentially, 60 mV a decade, until the series resistance takes over; reverse, only the small saturation current flows until breakdown.
labs.lecture: Strasser (2015), section 5.3, pp. 133–141; Hobler (2009), part 1, p. 3

equations.eq: pn = pN exp(U/UT), np = nP exp(U/UT)
equations.note: minority densities at the zone's edges

equations.eq: Js = e ni² (Dp/(Lp ND) + Dn/(Ln NA))
equations.note: the saturation current density, long diode
at fixed forward voltage; 0.05 /K for Si at 0.7 V

equations.eq: I = Is (exp(Ud/(n UT)) − 1), U = Ud + I Rs
equations.note: ideality factor n (the collection takes n = 2) and a series resistance; the script names both effects (p. 137)

practice.question: Exercise 1.6: a 1.5 V source drives a diode through 1 Ω, and 0.7 V falls across the diode. With n = 2 and UT = 25 mV, what is its saturation current Is?
practice.source: Worked by hand from Hobler (2009), exercise 1.6 c, p. 6, with its diode data on p. 3; agrees with the collection's solutions, p. 8 (665 nA)

practice.question: With the collection's n = 2 and UT = 25 mV, by how much must the voltage rise for the forward current to grow tenfold?
practice.solution: I ∝ e^(U/(n UT)), so ΔU = n UT ln 10 = 2 × 25 mV × 2.303 = 115 mV a decade; the ideal diode (n = 1) needs about 60 mV.
practice.source: Worked by hand from Strasser (2015), p. 137, and Hobler (2009), p. 3

labs.title: The bipolar transistor's output characteristics
labs.idea: The base–emitter voltage sets the electrons injected into a thin base; the collector collects them whatever its voltage, so the transistor is a current source, until the collector junction too turns forward.
labs.lecture: Strasser (2015), section 6.1, pp. 161–168; Hobler (2009), part 2, p. 17

equations.note: diffusion across a thin base of width W

practice.question: Exercise 2.1: a common-emitter stage on U0 = 5 V should carry IC0 = 10 mA with its output resting at Ua0 = 3 V. What collector resistor RC does it need?
practice.source: Hobler (2009), exercise 2.1 a, p. 17; agrees with the course's worked solutions (Lösungswege, p. 12)

practice.question: What is that stage's small-signal voltage gain vu, with UT = 25 mV?
practice.source: Hobler (2009), exercise 2.1 b, p. 17; agrees with the course's worked solutions (Lösungswege, p. 12)

labs.title: The MOSFET: threshold and output characteristics
labs.idea: Above the threshold voltage the gate holds a channel of electrons at the surface; the drain current grows with UDS until the channel pinches off at its drain end, and is then constant.
labs.law: ID = β((UGS − Ut)UDS − UDS²/2),  then ID = β/2 (UGS − Ut)²
labs.lecture: Strasser (2015), sections 6.2.2–6.2.3, pp. 174–188; Hobler (2009), part 3, pp. 47–48

equations.note: the Fermi potential of the substrate; the script prints kBT/(q ln(NA/ni)), a misprint
the threshold: work function, oxide charge, bulk charge, band bending

equations.eq: QB = −√(2 εSi e NA (2ΦF + USB)), Cox = εox/dox
equations.note: the bulk charge, with the substrate voltage; negative, as p. 183 says (p. 184 prints its magnitude)

equations.eq: ID = β((UGS − Ut)UDS − ½UDS²) for UDS ≤ UGS − Ut; ID = β/2 (UGS − Ut)² beyond
equations.tex: I_\mathrm{D} = \beta\Big((U_\mathrm{GS} - U_\mathrm{t})U_\mathrm{DS} - \tfrac{1}{2}U_\mathrm{DS}^2\Big) \ \text{for } U_\mathrm{DS} \le U_\mathrm{GS} - U_\mathrm{t}, \qquad I_\mathrm{D} = \frac{\beta}{2}(U_\mathrm{GS} - U_\mathrm{t})^2 \ \text{beyond}, \qquad \beta = \frac{\mu C_\mathrm{ox}W}{L}
equations.note: the output characteristics, β = µ Cox W/L
the transconductance in the current-source region

practice.question: A source follower: the gate rests at Ue0 = 4 V and the n-MOS (Ut = 1 V, β = 2.5 mA/V²) carries 1 mA in its current-source region. What is the output (source) voltage Ua0?
practice.solution: ID = β/2 (UGS − Ut)², so UGS = Ut + √(2ID/β) = 1 V + √0.8 V = 1.89 V; Ua0 = Ue0 − UGS = 2.11 V.
practice.source: Elektronische Bauelemente, Beispiel 5.1 (source follower), as in the course's worked solutions (Lösungswege, p. 47)

practice.question: Exercise 3.3: a self-conducting n-MOS (Ut = −3 V, β = 2 mA/V²) has its gate and source at 0 V and its drain through RD to U0 = 12 V. Which RD puts it exactly at the edge of the ohmic region?
practice.solution: UGS = 0, so ID = β/2 (0 − Ut)² = 1 mA/V² × 9 V² = 9 mA. The edge is UDS = UGS − Ut = 3 V, so RD = (12 V − 3 V)/9 mA = 1 kΩ.
practice.source: Worked by hand from Hobler (2009), exercise 3.3 a, p. 48; agrees with the collection's solutions, p. 56 (1 kΩ)

labs.title: The common-emitter stage
labs.idea: The base drive sets the collector current exponentially and the collector resistor turns it into a voltage: a steep, bent transfer curve. An emitter resistor straightens it and trades gain for a gain set by resistors.
labs.law: A = −S RC / (1 + S RE),  S = IC/UT

equations.eq: A = −S RC/(1 + S RE) ≈ −RC/RE for S RE ≫ 1
ue = UT ln(IC/Is) + IC RE, ua = U0 − IC RC

practice.question: A common-emitter stage carries IC = 1 mA, with RC = 5 kΩ and RE = 1 kΩ. With UT = 25 mV, what is its small-signal gain?
practice.solution: S = IC/UT = 40 mS, S RE = 40, so A = −S RC/(1 + S RE) = −200/41 = −4.88; the approximation −RC/RE gives −5.
practice.source: Worked by hand from Zimmermann (2010), (1.4)

labs.title: The current source and its output resistance
labs.idea: A transistor's output curves are nearly flat, so it delivers a nearly constant current; the Early effect tilts them. Feedback through an emitter resistor raises the output resistance up to β times.
labs.law: ra = rCE (1 + β RE/(RE + rBE)),  rCE = UA/Ia

equations.note: the plain transistor, by its Early voltage

equations.eq: ra ≈ rCE (1 + S RE) for RE ≪ rBE; β rCE for RE ≫ rBE
equations.tex: r_\mathrm{a} \approx \begin{cases} r_\mathrm{CE}(1 + SR_\mathrm{E}) & \text{for } R_\mathrm{E} \ll r_\mathrm{BE} \\ \beta r_\mathrm{CE} & \text{for } R_\mathrm{E} \gg r_\mathrm{BE} \end{cases}

equations.note: the small-signal circuit solved; its two limits are (1.19)

practice.question: A current source delivers 1 mA through a transistor with UA = 100 V and β = 100, with RE = 100 kΩ, far above rBE. What is its output resistance? (UT = 25 mV)
practice.solution: rCE = UA/Ia = 100 kΩ, rBE = β UT/Ia = 2.5 kΩ; ra = rCE (1 + β RE/(RE + rBE)) = 100 kΩ × (1 + 100 × 0.976) = 9.86 MΩ, close to the limit β rCE = 10 MΩ of (1.19).
practice.source: Worked by hand from Zimmermann (2010), (1.13) and (1.19)

labs.title: Push-pull output stages
labs.idea: Two complementary emitter followers take turns: in class B neither conducts at rest, which saves power but leaves a dead zone at the crossing; a small bias (class AB) removes it. The efficiency rises with the swing, to 78.5 %.
labs.law: PL = Ûa²/(2RL),  PB = 2 UB Ûa/(π RL),  η = (π/4) Ûa/UB
labs.lecture: Zimmermann (2010), section 2.2, pp. 16–25; Schneider & Zimmermann (2005), example 1

equations.note: class A emitter follower, RL = RE, swing to −UB/2

equations.eq: PT,max at Ûa = 2UB/π = 0.637 UB; PT,max = 0.32 PB,max
equations.note: both transistors; the worst case for the heat sink
per transistor, at its worst amplitude

equations.eq: Is (e^((ue + Ub/2 − ua)/UT) − e^((ua − ue + Ub/2)/UT)) = ua/RL
equations.note: the transfer curve: the npn's current less the pnp's flows into RL; Ub = 0 is class B

practice.question: A class B push-pull stage is to deliver 25 W of sine into 8 Ω. What output amplitude does that take?
practice.solution: PL = Ûa²/(2RL), so Ûa = √(2 × 25 W × 8 Ω) = 20 V; with 2–3 V left across the transistor the supply is UB = 22 V.
practice.source: Schneider & Zimmermann (2005), example 1, B1/1; agrees with its worked solution

practice.question: With UB = 22 V and RL = 8 Ω, what is the largest loss in one of the two transistors?
practice.solution: The loss peaks at Ûa = 2UB/π; there PvT,max = UB²/(π² RL) = 484/(9.87 × 8) W = 6.13 W, about 6 W per transistor.
practice.source: Schneider & Zimmermann (2005), example 1, B1/3; agrees with its worked solution (about 6 W)

labs.title: The op-amp's loop gain and phase margin
labs.idea: Feedback trades gain for bandwidth, keeping their product. Where the loop gain falls to one, the phase left over decides whether the step response settles calmly or rings; a follower is the hardest case.
labs.law: vr = vg/(1 + β vg),  margin = 180° + arg(β vg) where |β vg| = 1
labs.lecture: Zimmermann (2010), section 4.1, pp. 69–77; Schneider & Zimmermann (2005), example 6

equations.note: one pole; the lab adds a second
the lab's loop, two poles; its step solved in closed form, checked against a simulation
the closed loop (4.4) with two poles: the second-order system whose step response is plotted

practice.question: Example 6 b: a loop gain vs = 10⁴ × 0.1 / ((1 + jω/100 s⁻¹)(1 + jω/1111 s⁻¹)). At which angular frequency is |vs| = 1?
practice.source: Schneider & Zimmermann (2005), example 6 c, B6/4; agrees with its worked solution (10 530 s⁻¹)

practice.question: What phase margin does that loop have?
practice.solution: arg vs = −arctan(105) − arctan(9.5) ≈ −174°, so the margin is about 6°: the circuit rings strongly before it settles.
practice.source: Schneider & Zimmermann (2005), example 6 c, B6/4; agrees with its worked solution (about 6°)

labs.title: Slew-rate limiting
labs.idea: The compensation capacitor charges only so fast, so the output never changes faster than the slew rate. A large, fast sine turns into a triangle long before the small-signal bandwidth is reached.

equations.note: the compensation capacitor charged by the input stage's current; 0.6 V/µs for the 741

equations.eq: dua/dt max = Ûa ω, at the zero crossing
Ûa,max = SR/(2π f) for f > fp

equations.note: the lab's follower: its loop of bandwidth fT, its rate limited to SR

practice.question: A 741 slews at 0.6 V/µs. Up to which frequency can it deliver an undistorted sine of 10 V amplitude?
practice.solution: fp = SR/(2π Ûa) = 0.6 V/µs / (2π × 10 V) = 9.5 kHz, which the script rounds to 10 kHz.
practice.source: Zimmermann (2010), section 4.4, p. 86, its worked example

practice.question: What amplitude can that op-amp still deliver undistorted at 100 kHz?
practice.solution: Ûa = SR/(2π f) = 0.6·10⁶ V/s / (2π × 10⁵ /s) = 0.95 V, which the script rounds to 1 V.
practice.source: Zimmermann (2010), section 4.4, p. 86, its worked example

labs.title: Thermal and shot noise
labs.idea: A resistor's electrons jitter with heat; a current crossing a barrier arrives in single charges. Both make white, Gaussian noise that grows with the square root of the bandwidth.
labs.law: v² = 4 kT R Δf,  i² = 2 q I Δf

equations.note: open-circuit thermal noise of a resistor

equations.eq: kB T0 = 4·10⁻²¹ W/Hz at T0 = 290 K

equations.note: where the two are equal; the script's example: 1 kΩ at 300 K matches the shot noise of 50 µA

practice.question: A diode carries 1 mA. What is its shot-noise current (RMS) in a bandwidth of 1 MHz?
practice.solution: i² = 2 q I Δf = 2 × 1.6·10⁻¹⁹ C × 10⁻³ A × 10⁶ Hz = 3.2·10⁻¹⁶ A², so i = 1.8·10⁻⁸ A RMS.
practice.source: Zimmermann (2010), section 6.3, (6.12), p. 133, its worked example

practice.question: What is the thermal noise voltage (RMS) of a 1 kΩ resistor at 300 K in 10 kHz?
practice.source: Worked by hand from Zimmermann (2010), (6.1)

labs.title: A 25 W amplifier, from the supply to the heat sink
labs.idea: One amplifier, sized the way the worked example sizes it: the supply for 25 W into 8 Ω, the worst loss in each output transistor, the heat sink that keeps their junctions below 150 °C, and the class-AB bias that grows as the transistors heat up.
labs.law: Ûa = √(2 PL RL)    PvT,max = UB²/(π² RL) ≈ 0.1 UB²/RL    PT = (Tj − Tk)/(RthB + RthK)    IC0 = (UB0 − 2UBE)/(R1 + R2)
labs.lecture: Zimmermann (2010), section 2.2, pp. 16–31; Schneider & Zimmermann (2005), Beispiel 1, B1/1–B1/6; Strasser (2015), section 6.1, p. 166

practice.question: A class-B stage drives 25 W into 8 Ω with UB = 22 V. Each BD243/BD244 loses at most 6 W; RthJC = 1.92 K/W, Tj,max = 150 °C. What may the case temperature be at most?
practice.solution: ϑG,max = Tj,max − PTot·RthJC = 150 °C − 6 W · 1.92 K/W = 138.48 °C.
practice.source: Schneider & Zimmermann (2005), Beispiel 1, B1/4

practice.question: Each transistor sits on a mica washer of 0.5 K/W, both on one heat sink, in air at 50 °C. What thermal resistance may the heat sink have at most?
practice.solution: ϑKB = 138.5 °C − 0.5 K/W · 6 W = 135.5 °C; the sink carries 12 W, so Rth,KB-U = (135.5 − 50) K/12 W = 7.125 K/W.
practice.source: Schneider & Zimmermann (2005), Beispiel 1, B1/5

practice.question: Two diodes give UB0 = 1.2 V between the bases, the hot transistors need 2UBE = 1.0 V, and R1 + R2 = 1 Ω. What quiescent current flows?
practice.solution: The 200 mV left over drive IC0 = 0.2 V/1 Ω = 200 mA, four times the 50 mA set cold.
practice.source: Zimmermann (2010), section 2.2, p. 30
